#### F3_semantic_groups_table
| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Assertion-of-truth expressions / Reality-asserting expressions / Propositional truth assertion and denial | These expressions are used by a speaker to affirm that a proposition corresponds to fact, or to frame a statement as sincere and accurate. They appear in contexts where the speaker is either making a direct claim of truth or intensifying the credibility of what they are saying, including in response to claims, in argument, and in contexts where a speaker is committing to or challenging the factual status of a proposition. They contrast with expressions in the falsehood/deception group and are distinct from correctness expressions, which evaluate correctness of procedures or documents rather than propositional truth. | *kweli*; *ukweli*; *kweli kweli*; *kwa kweli*; *kwa kweli kweli*; *kweli kabisa*; *kweli ni kweli*; *Hii ni kweli*; *hakika*; *kwa hakika*; *bila shaka*; *dhahiri*; *Nakuambia kweli*; *ni kweli*; *si kweli*; *ni kweli kabisa kwamba...*; *kweli au uongo*; *Je, ni kweli?*; *ukweli ni kwamba...*; *ukweli wa mambo ni kwamba...*; *ni sahihi*; *si sahihi*; *sahihi kabisa*; *haki kabisa!*; *ukweli mtupu*; *ukweli wote*; *sahihi sahihi*; *sawa*; *sawa sawa*; *ni dhahiri kwamba…*; *kwa dhahiri*; *hali halisi*; *halisi*; *haki* (in truth-asserting uses); *haki ya Mungu*; *ukweli wa Mungu* | *hakika* and *bila shaka* also appear in the certainty/reliability group; *kweli kweli* and *kwa kweli* also appear in Group 2; *halisi* also appears in Group 8; *haki* also appears in rights/justice and moral rightness groups; *dhahiri* also appears in Group 6; *sawa* also overlaps with moral fairness group | Within this group, there is a further distinction in usage between expressions that assert truth of a statement (*kweli*, *sahihi*, *sawa*) and expressions that assert the genuineness of an object or situation (*halisi*, *hali halisi*). *Sahihi* is used of answers, documents, and calculations; *halisi* is used of gold, goods, and persons. *Dhahiri* is distinctive in that it asserts self-evidence rather than simple accuracy. *Haki kabisa* is used as an affirmative response particle in spoken Swahili and overlaps with the rights/justice group, but its use as a truth-affirmation response is well attested. |
| Sincerity framing in discourse | These expressions are used at the beginning of utterances, or parenthetically, to signal that the speaker is being honest or genuine — not to assert the truth of a specific proposition, but to frame the entire speech act as sincere. They function as discourse markers rather than as predicates. | *kwa kweli*; *kwa kweli, sijui*; *kusema ukweli*; *kusema ukweli, sikupenda hilo*; *kweli kweli, hii ni ajabu*; *kwa kweli kweli* | *kwa kweli* and *kweli kweli* also appear in Group 1 | The distinction observed in usage is that in Group 1 these expressions modify a specific propositional claim, while here they frame the speaker's overall stance. *Kusema ukweli* as a parenthetical is particularly characteristic of this group and does not appear in Group 1 usage. |
| Certainty and reliability expressions | These expressions are used to evaluate whether a piece of information, a source, or a claim can be relied upon or is known with confidence. They appear in epistemic contexts where the speaker is assessing how sure they or others are, and they contrast with *shaka* (doubt) and *bila uhakika* (without certainty). They differ from Group 1 in that they focus on the epistemic status of the knower or source rather than on the propositional content of a claim. | *uhakika*; *hakika*; *bila uhakika*; *kwa uhakika*; *hakika kabisa*; *Nina uhakika*; *Sina uhakika*; *shaka*; *bila shaka*; *kuhakikisha*; *uhakikisho*; *uaminifu wa chanzo*; *uaminifu wa habari* | *kuhakikisha* and *uhakikisho* also appear in Group 6; *hakika* and *bila shaka* also appear in Group 1 | *kuhakikisha* is used in both everyday procedural contexts (making sure a door is closed) and in epistemic verification contexts (confirming a fact). The procedural uses do not involve truth evaluation at all, which means this verb spans this group and contexts entirely outside the truth domain. |
| Correctness and accuracy expressions / Accuracy and correctness evaluation | These expressions are used to evaluate whether a statement, calculation, document, answer, or procedure meets a standard of accuracy or correctness. They are particularly common in educational, administrative, legal, scientific, and technical contexts. They differ from Group 1 in that they evaluate against a standard or norm (correct/incorrect) rather than asserting correspondence to fact in a general sense. They are frequently applied to specific domains by the pattern *X sahihi* or *usahihi wa X*. | *sahihi*; *usahihi*; *Ni sahihi*; *Si sahihi*; *sahihi kabisa*; *jibu sahihi*; *taarifa sahihi*; *nakala sahihi*; *sahihi na kamili*; *tarehe sahihi*; *kwa usahihi*; *kwa usahihi zaidi*; *kwa usahihi zaidi, idadi ni elfu tatu, si mbili*; *usahihi wa takwimu*; *usahihi wa lugha*; *usahihi wa habari*; *usahihi wa tafsiri*; *usahihi wa taarifa*; *usahihi wa kipimo*; *kusahihisha*; *kusahihishwa*; *usahihishaji*; *msahihishaji / wasahihishaji*; *takwimu sahihi*; *matamshi sahihi*; *sarufi sahihi*; *tafsiri sahihi*; *hesabu sahihi*; *maelezo sahihi*; *lugha sahihi*; *utambuzi sahihi*; *thibitisha usahihi*; *kuhakikisha usahihi*; *jibu lako si sahihi — jaribu tena*; *taarifa hii imethibitishwa kuwa sahihi*; *hakikisha kuwa taarifa ni sahihi kabla ya kuisambaza*; *sahihisha makosa*; *hii si sahihi*; *sahihi sahihi* | *kusahihisha* also appears in Group 6 when used of document validation | *sahihi* also has a distinct use as "signature" (see Group 7), which is a separate usage cluster. The correctness/accuracy cluster is the dominant one in terms of frequency and range of contexts. The pattern *kwa usahihi zaidi* as a precision-correction frame is particularly characteristic. |
| Falsehood, deception, and inauthenticity expressions | These expressions are used to identify a statement, object, or person as false, deceptive, or not genuine, and to characterize acts, persons, or patterns of conduct as involving deliberate deception, misleading, or fraud. They appear in contexts of accusation, moral condemnation, legal evaluation, commercial fraud detection, and narrative contexts where the intentional production of false impressions is at issue. Several of these expressions contrast directly with authenticity expressions in Group 7. | *uongo*; *Hii ni uongo*; *Piga uongo*; *Anapiga uongo*; *kusema uongo*; *uongo mtupu*; *uongo wa wazi*; *Uongo una miguu mifupi*; *Uongo ni dhambi*; *kusema uongo ni dhambi*; *kueneza uongo*; *amejaa uongo*; *uongo wake ulidhihirika*; *kudanganya*; *udanganyifu*; *danganyifu*; *mdanganyifu / wadanganyifu*; *kudanganywa*; *kudanganyika*; *alikudanganya kwa makusudi*; *kudanganya kwa maneno na matendo*; *alidanganywa na macho yake mwenyewe*; *udanganyifu wake ulifunuliwa hadharani*; *kujikinga na udanganyifu*; *ghushi*; *kughushi*; *mghushi / waghushi*; *Hii ni ghushi*; *Si kweli*; *nusu ukweli*; *ulaghai*; *mlaghai*; *kulaghai*; *kesi ya ulaghai*; *alishtakiwa kwa ulaghai*; *muongo*; *waongo*; *shahidi wa uongo*; *imani potofu*; *muongo wa hali ya juu* | *bandia* overlaps with this group but is treated as the core of Group 8; *ghushi* overlaps with both this group and Group 8; *nusu ukweli* is a borderline item | *uongo* is primarily used of statements and verbal acts; *bandia* is primarily used of objects, documents, and physical goods. *udanganyifu* and *kudanganya* emphasize the deliberate, intentional character of the deception, whereas *uongo* can describe a false statement without necessarily implying intent. *muongo* and *mdanganyifu* are agentive forms that characterize persons rather than acts or objects. *ulaghai* is more specific than *udanganyifu*, carrying connotations of material fraud and appearing more in legal contexts. The distinction between *uongo* (falsehood as a state or product) and *kudanganya* (the act of deceiving) is consistently maintained in usage. The construction *ukweli nusu ni uongo* explicitly bridges this group and Group 1. |
| Verification, confirmation, and proof expressions | These expressions are used when a speaker or institution acts to establish, confirm, or demonstrate that something is true, authentic, or correct. They appear in legal, administrative, academic, journalistic, and everyday procedural contexts. | Direct truth predication / Predicate assertions of truth and falsehood | These expressions are used as complete or near-complete utterances to assert that a statement, claim, or situation is true or false. They appear in contexts of testimony, dispute, and everyday affirmation, and they typically take the direct evidential enclitic *-m/-mi* or the negative polar *-chu*. Their primary function is to commit the speaker to a position on the truth-value of something. They appear primarily as predicates in simple declarative constructions, where a speaker asserts or denies that something is true, genuine, or false, and they are used in direct response to questions about whether something is the case. | *cheqam*; *cheqami*; *cheqa*; *cheqaq*; *cheqam kay*; *cheqapuni*; *cheqaqpuni*; *cheqataq*; *mana cheqachu*; *manan cheqachu*; *mana cheqa*; *mana cheqaq*; *llullam*; *llulla*; *mana llullachu*; *manan llullachu*; *cheqachus?*; *cheqachus, manachus?*; *llullachu?*; *pantasqam*; *sut'im*; *sut'imi*; *mana sut'ichu*; *manan sut'ichu*; *chiqapmi* [UNCERTAIN]; *chiqap cheqam*; *cheqallam*; *kikinmi*; *kikinllam*; *mana kikinchu*; *hinam*; *hinami*; *allinmi*; *chiqan*; *allin*; *mana allin*; *mana chiqan*; *mana sut'i*; *kikin*; *qelqasqa*; *cheqam, arím*; *allinmi, cheqam*; *iñiymi, cheqam*; *yachanim / yachaninim*; *manan pantanichu*; *manan yachanichu*; *manan iñinichu*; *manan riqsinichunim*; *manan llullakuyta atinichu*; *cheqanchasqam*; *cheqanchasqa* | *pantasqam* and *sut'im* participate in this group but also appear in other groups. *Qelqasqa* is included here because it appears in the same predicate construction type, though its primary meaning (being documented/written) is distinct from the others. Some items (e.g., *manan yachanichu*, *manan riqsinichunim*) are conventionalized testimonial formulas for denying knowledge or recognition rather than denying the truth of a proposition per se. | The direct evidential clitic *-m/-mi* is not merely an intensifier but a grammatical marker of the speaker's epistemic commitment. The paired constructions (*cheqam, arím*; *allinmi, cheqam*; *iñiymi, cheqam*) represent an attested rhetorical pattern of reinforcing an assertion by combining two evidentially marked affirmatives. |
| Evaluation of speech as truthful or deceptive / Enjoinment and description of truthful communication / Terms associated with the truthfulness or falsity of speech acts | These expressions are used specifically to evaluate a speech act or a speaker's words as honest, accurate, deceptive, or false. They appear in legal testimony, moral instruction, and everyday contexts where the reliability of what someone says is at issue. The target of evaluation is the speech act itself or the words produced, not a state of affairs in the world. They are also used in contexts where truthful speech is being required, described, or characterized as an action, and in imperative constructions requesting truthful speech. They are distinguished from Group 1 in that they are oriented toward the act of speaking rather than toward the truth-value of a proposition. | *cheqata rimay*; *cheqanta rimay*; *cheqata rimani*; *cheqa simi*; *cheqa rimay*; *llulla simi*; *llulla rimay*; *llulla nispa rimay*; *cheqa nispa rimay*; *mana cheqam nispa rimay*; *sut'ita rimay*; *sut'ita rimani*; *allin rimay*; *allin simi*; *kikin simiwan rimay*; *cheqam, Diospa sutimpi*; *cheqaqta rimay*; *cheqaqta willaway*; *cheqaqtam rimasqanki*; *chiqan rimay*; *chiqap rimay* [UNCERTAIN]; *llulla willay* [UNCERTAIN]; *willakuy*; *cheqaqmi nin*; *llullam nin*; *llullam willakurqa*; *cheqa willay*; *sut'i simi*; *sut'i willay*; *allintam rimay*; *cheqanta rimayta munay*; *cheqanta rimanayki tiyan*; *sut'itatam rimanayki tiyan*; *cheqa kasqanta willay*; *cheqa kasqanman hina rimay*; *yachaq kaspa rimay*; *cheqanta rimay* vs. *mana yachaspa rimay*; *llulla willakuy* | *Allin rimay* and *allin simi* overlap with Group 5 (moral characterization of persons) but appear here specifically in speech-evaluation contexts. *Cheqa simi* and *llulla simi* are direct contrasts within this group. | *Rimay* and *willakuy* are not themselves P1 items in the truth-evaluation domain but appear as the verbal heads in these constructions. *Simi* ("word, speech") collocations (*cheqa simi*, *llulla simi*) are included here because their primary attested context is the evaluation of speech acts. The deontic constructions (*cheqanta rimanayki tiyan*, *sut'itatam rimanayki tiyan*) are included because they appear in the same discourse contexts (legal testimony, moral instruction) as the descriptive expressions, and they specify the same action (truthful speech) as obligatory. The imperative constructions (*Cheqaqta rimay*, *Cheqaqta willaway*) are specifically attested in this group and not in others, suggesting that the enjoining of truthful speech is a distinct usage context. |

They are distinct from simple truth predication (Group 1) in that they describe a process rather than a result. They are distinguished from Group 1 (which involves asserting truth or falsehood) in that they describe processes or actions directed at establishing or restoring correctness, rather than simply stating that something is or is not true. | *cheqanchay*; # G1 — Cross-Language Summary of Observed Semantic Organization

---

## 1. Language Inventory

- **zh** (Chinese, Mandarin) — A large, morphologically isolating language with extensive compounding and a productive *-性* nominalization suffix; the data covers a wide range of truth, accuracy, authenticity, and deception vocabulary across everyday, legal, journalistic, and philosophical registers.
- **he** (Hebrew, Modern) — A Semitic language with root-and-pattern morphology; the data shows extensive derivation from a small number of roots (especially א-מ-נ and א-מ-ת), a productive *-ut* abstract nominalization suffix, and a distinctive *ʾi-* negation prefix on nominalizations.
- **sa** (Sanskrit) — A classical Indo-European language with highly productive compounding and suffixation; the data covers Vedic, epic, philosophical (Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Advaita Vedānta, Sāṃkhya), legal (Dharmaśāstra), and grammatical registers, with a strong emphasis on epistemological and ontological distinctions.
- **el** (Greek, Modern) — An Indo-European language with productive prefixal negation (ἀν-/α-), *-ότητα* abstract nominalization, and a distinctive etymological connection between the word for truth (*αλήθεια*) and unconcealment; the data covers everyday, legal, journalistic, philosophical, and religious registers.
- **en** (English) — A Germanic language with mixed Latinate and native vocabulary; the data shows productive prefixal negation (*un-*, *in-*, *dis-*), *-ity/-ness/-hood* abstract nominalization, and a large set of fixed verbal idioms (*ring true*, *come true*, *hold true*).
- **tl** (Tagalog) — An Austronesian language with a complex affix system (circumfixes, focus-marking prefixes, aspect infixes); the data shows the *ka-…-an* circumfix as the primary abstract nominalizer, particle-marked epistemic stance constructions, and a distinctive set of discourse particles (*ba*, *na*, *pala*, *nga*, *naman*).
- **sw** (Swahili) — A Bantu language with noun-class agreement morphology; the data shows the *u-* prefix as the primary abstract nominalizer, productive *-sha/-isha* causative derivation, and a large set of Arabic loanwords in the truth-evaluation domain.
- **qu** (Quechua, Southern) — An Andean language with agglutinative morphology and a grammaticalized evidentiality system (*-m/-mi*, *-s/-si*, *-chá*); the data shows the *-ncha-* causative verbalizer, *-ka-* intransitive verbalizer, and *-q* agentive nominalizer as productive derivational strategies.

---

## 2. Per-Language Semantic Sketch

### 2.1 Chinese (zh)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data distinguishes at least five overlapping but distinct evaluative dimensions: (1) factual truth of statements (*真实*, *失实*, *属实*); (2) genuineness of objects and documents (*真伪*, *假冒*, *伪造*); (3) correspondence between name/label and actual nature (*名副其实*, *本质*, *实质*); (4) correctness relative to a standard (*正确*, *错误*, *准确*); and (5) reliability of sources and persons (*可靠*, *诚实*). The root 真 (*zhēn*) is highly productive and participates in all five dimensions, while 假 (*jiǎ*) and 伪 (*wěi*) are more restricted to inauthenticity and deliberate falsification respectively. The 实 (*shí*) family (实际, 事实, 真实, 失实) forms a distinct cluster oriented toward factual reality and practical grounding.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *-性* suffix is highly productive for abstract nominalization (*真实性*, *可靠性*, *正确性*) but is not available for monosyllabic roots or verbal items. The *-化* suffix is productive for causative/process nominalizations (*合法化*, *道德化*) but is marginal for most truth-domain adjectives. The *-者* agentive suffix is attested primarily for negative-pole agents (*伪造者*, *欺骗者*) with no parallel positive-pole agentive (*truth-teller*) via this suffix. The *-感* suffix (*真实感*) is distinct from *-性* in denoting experiential/aesthetic properties.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The *是…的* copular frame is the default predication construction. Discourse-initial frames (*实际上*, *本质上*, *事实上*) are highly grammaticalized as sentence-level adverbials. The *如实* + verb pattern is a productive adverbial construction for truthful reporting. Regulatory prohibitive constructions (*严禁弄虚作假*, *不得造假*) are restricted to the deliberate-falsification sub-domain.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The 真/假 binary is the foundational lexical opposition. The 正确/错误 pair is the primary correctness opposition. The 客观/主观 pair is the primary objectivity opposition. Several constructional oppositions are attested: 揭露真相 vs. 掩盖真相; 尊重事实 vs. 歪曲事实. The *名副其实* / *名不副实* pair is formed by internal negation of a fixed four-character expression.

---

### 2.2 Hebrew (he)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data shows a dense root family centered on א-מ-נ (*ʾ-m-n*: trust, faithfulness, reliability) and א-מ-ת (*ʾ-m-t*: truth, genuineness). These two roots are semantically adjacent but distinct: א-מ-ת is oriented toward factual truth and authenticity of statements and objects, while א-מ-נ covers trustworthiness, reliability, faithfulness, and belief. The data distinguishes: (1) propositional truth (*ʾemet*, *nakhon*); (2) precision (*meduyaq*, *diyyuq*); (3) reliability of persons and sources (*ʾamin*, *mehiman*, *neʾeman*); (4) legal validity (*taqef*, *batel*, *kasher*, *pasul*); (5) legitimacy (*legitimi*, *ḥuqi*); and (6) sincerity (*kanut*, *yashar*). The *kasher/pasul* pair is distinctive in combining ritual fitness with legal admissibility.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *-ut* suffix is the primary abstract nominalizer (*ʾaminut*, *neʾemanut*, *mehimanut*). The *ʾi-* prefix is productive for negating *-ut* nominalizations in formal registers (*ʾi-diyyuq*, *ʾi-sevirut*, *ʾi-ḥuqiyyut*). The *bilti* negator is used for formal adjectival negation of loanwords (*bilti savir*, *bilti legitimi*). The *-an* agentive suffix is attested for *shaqran* (liar) and *dayqan* (precise person) but not for a positive truth-telling agent. The *ʾi-* prefix on nominalizations has acquired particular institutional salience in Israeli administrative law (*ʾi-sevirut qitsunit*).

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The zero-copula nominal predicate is the unmarked present-tense attribution pattern. The *nakhon she-* concessive frame is a highly frequent discourse pattern in argumentation. The *ha-ʾemet hi she-* frame is a standard corrective/clarifying construction. The *lehitgalaʾh ke-* construction is the primary inchoative for discovery that something is true or false. The *be-* + abstract noun adverbial pattern (*beʾemet*, *bediyyuq*) is highly productive, with *bediyyuq* having grammaticalized as a precision adverb beyond the truth domain.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *ʾemet/sheqer* pair is the foundational lexical opposition. The *kasher/pasul* pair is a distinctive lexical opposition in the legal-religious domain. The *nimtsa mehiman/nimtsa lo mehiman* constructional pair is institutionally fixed in legal judgments. The *ʾi-* prefix on nominalizations produces a productive set of negated abstract nouns (*ʾi-sevirut*, *ʾi-diyyuq*, *ʾi-ḥuqiyyut*) that have no direct parallel in the adjectival negation system.

### 2.3 Sanskrit (sa)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data shows the most elaborate set of semantic distinctions among all languages in the corpus. Key distinctions include: (1) propositional truth of statements (*satya*, *tathya*, *yathārtha*); (2) cosmic/moral order (*ṛta*, *dharma*); (3) ontological status of being (*sat*, *asat*, *mithyā*); (4) valid cognition and its sources (*pramā*, *pramāṇa*, *prāmāṇya*); (5) error and illusion (*bhrama*, *bhrānti*, *viparyaya*); (6) grammatical correctness (*sādhu*, *apaśabda*); (7) contextual appropriateness (*yukta*, *ucita*, *aucitya*); and (8) levels of reality (*paramārtha*, *vyāvahārika*). The *sat/asat* opposition is both ontological and evaluative. The *mithyā* category in Advaita Vedānta introduces a third ontological value (neither real nor unreal) that disrupts the binary.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *-tā* and *-tva* suffixes are both productive abstract nominalizers with no consistent semantic distinction between them. The *-vādin* compound suffix is the dominant agentive pattern (*satyavādin*, *asatyavādin*) and is more productive than *-bhāṣin* or *-jña* in this domain. The *ābhāsa* suffix/compound element systematically marks pseudo-instances (*pramāṇābhāsa*, *hetvābhāsa*). The *svataḥ/parataḥ* opposition within the compound frame *prāmāṇya* encodes a specific intra-school epistemological debate.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The zero-copula nominal sentence is the unmarked predication pattern. The *-taḥ* adverbial (*vastutaḥ*, *tattvataḥ*, *paramārthataḥ*) is a distinctive discourse-marking construction for asserting the level of analysis at which a claim is made. The prescriptive optative (*satyaṃ brūyāt*) and gerundive (*satyāt na pramaditavyam*) are the standard forms for ethical injunctions. The ablative deviation construction (*satyāt na pracalati*) is a productive pattern for expressing steadfast adherence to a normative standard. The *jāyate/utpadyate* constructions for cognitive arising and *nivartate* for cognitive cessation are domain-specific inchoative patterns.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *satya/asatya*, *sat/asat*, *pramā/apramā*, *pramāṇa/apramāṇa*, *dharma/adharma*, *sādhu/asādhu* pairs are all formed by prefixal negation (*a-/an-*). The *satkāryavāda/asatkāryavāda* pair encodes opposing philosophical positions. The *mukhya/gauṇa* and *mukhya/aupacārika* pairs encode the literal/figurative distinction in Mīmāṃsā. The *svataḥprāmāṇya/parataḥprāmāṇya* pair is unique in encoding an intra-school debate within a single compound frame.

### 2.4 Greek, Modern (el)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data distinguishes: (1) propositional truth (*αληθής*, *αλήθεια*, *αληθινός*); (2) accuracy and precision (*ακριβής*, *ακρίβεια*); (3) genuineness of objects and documents (*γνήσιος*, *αυθεντικός*, *πρωτότυπο* vs. *πλαστός*, *νόθος*); (4) legal validity (*έγκυρος*, *άκυρος*); (5) credibility of sources and witnesses (*αξιόπιστος*, *αναξιόπιστος*); (6) verisimilitude (*αληθοφανής*, *αληθοφάνεια*); and (7) surface appearance vs. reality (*φαινομενικός*, *δήθεν*, *τάχα*). The *αληθ-* root is highly productive and participates in all registers from everyday speech to philosophy and liturgy. The *γνήσιος/νόθος* pair encodes legitimate vs. illegitimate origin, while *αυθεντικός/πλαστός* encodes genuine vs. forged.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *-ότητα* suffix is the primary abstract nominalizer (*γνησιότητα*, *αυθεντικότητα*, *εγκυρότητα*). The *αν-/α-* privative prefix is productive for adjectival negation (*αναξιόπιστος*, *αναληθής*, *ανακριβής*). The *ψευδο-* prefix is a productive pseudo-compound element (*ψευδοεπιστήμη*, *ψευδοδίλημμα*). The agentive *ψεύτης* (liar) is well-established, but no parallel agentive for "truth-teller" is lexicalized; the concept requires periphrasis. The *γνησιοποίηση* (certification of genuineness) is a distinctive administrative nominalization.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The *αποδείχτηκε* + adjective construction is the primary inchoative for truth-value transitions. The *η αλήθεια είναι ότι* frame is a highly frequent corrective/clarifying construction. The *ψευδο-* compound pattern is freely productive. The *δήθεν* and *φερόμενος ως* constructions are distinctive epistemic hedge markers. The *γίνομαι* + adjective construction is noted as less natural than *αποδείχτηκε* for truth-value transitions specifically.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *αληθής/ψευδής* and *αλήθεια/ψεύδος* pairs are the foundational lexical oppositions. The *έγκυρος/άκυρος* pair is formed from a shared root with different prefixes rather than by simple privative negation. The *αληθοφανής/αληθής* opposition is distinctive in contrasting appearance of truth with actual truth. The *ψήφος εμπιστοσύνης/ψήφος δυσπιστίας* constructional pair is institutionally fixed in parliamentary discourse.

### 2.5 English (en)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data distinguishes: (1) propositional truth (*true*, *false*, *accurate*, *correct*); (2) genuineness of objects and persons (*genuine*, *authentic*, *bona fide* vs. *fake*, *counterfeit*, *spurious*); (3) legal and procedural validity (*valid*, *legitimate*, *rightful*); (4) reliability and credibility (*reliable*, *credible*, *trustworthy*); (5) sincerity (*sincere*, *honest*, *truthful*); (6) verisimilitude (*plausible*, *verisimilitude*, *apocryphal*); and (7) deliberate falsification (*fraudulent*, *fabricated*, *counterfeit*). The *true/false* binary is the most general. *Accurate* and *correct* are distinguished by degree-of-correspondence vs. conformity-to-norm. *Sincere* and *truthful* are distinguished by inner-state correspondence vs. statement-to-fact correspondence.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *-ity/-cy* suffixes are preferred for Latinate bases (*authenticity*, *validity*, *credibility*) while *-ness* is preferred for Germanic bases (*truthfulness*, *soundness*). The *un-* prefix is productive for Germanic bases (*untrue*, *untruthful*, *untrustworthy*) while *in-/im-/il-* is productive for Latinate bases (*inaccurate*, *invalid*, *illegitimate*). The agentive *-er* suffix is productive for negative-pole agents (*faker*, *counterfeiter*, *fabricator*) but the positive-pole "truth-teller" requires a compound form rather than simple suffixation. The *post-truth* compound is a recent formation with no parallel in other languages in the corpus.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The *prove* + adjective construction is the primary inchoative for truth-value transitions. The *it is true that … but* concessive frame is a highly frequent discourse pattern. The *to be honest* and *truth be told* parenthetical frames are grammaticalized sincerity markers. The *ring true/false*, *hold true*, *come true* verbal idioms are distinctive fixed constructions concentrated around the base form *true*. The *economical with the truth* idiom is a distinctive British English construction for misleading through omission.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *true/false* pair is the foundational lexical opposition. The *valid/sound* distinction in formal logic is a distinctive constructional contrast. The *accurate* (tolerates margin) vs. *exact* (no deviation) distinction is a lexical contrast within the fact-correspondence cluster. The *truthful* (habitual disposition of persons) vs. *true* (property of propositions) distributional contrast is explicitly documented.

### 2.6 Tagalog (tl)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data distinguishes: (1) factual truth of statements and situations (*totoo*, *katotohanan*); (2) genuineness and authenticity of objects and persons (*tunay*, *orihinal*, *awtentiko* vs. *huwad*, *peke*); (3) correctness (*tama*, *wasto*, *tumpak*); (4) honesty and sincerity of persons (*tapat*, *katapatan*); (5) loyalty and faithfulness (*katapatan*, *tiwala*); (6) credibility of sources and witnesses (*mapagkakatiwalaan*, *kredible*); and (7) deception (*sinungaling*, *kasinungalingan*, *linlang*). The *totoo/kasinungalingan* pair is the foundational truth/falsehood opposition. The root *tapat* covers both honesty of speech and loyalty/faithfulness to persons, a semantic range broader than any single English equivalent. The *huwad/peke* near-synonymy is distinguished primarily by register (formal/literary vs. colloquial).

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *ka-…-an* circumfix is the primary abstract nominalizer (*katotohanan*, *katapatan*, *katunayan*, *kasinungalingan*). The *pa-* + *tunay* + *-an* verbal paradigm (*patunayan*, *napatunayan*, *pinatunayan*) is the most grammaticalized causative in the truth domain. The *maka-* prefix (*makatotohanan*) derives adjectives meaning "in accordance with" a quality. The discourse particles (*ba*, *na*, *pala*, *nga*, *naman*) encode epistemic stance distinctions that are grammaticalized in Tagalog but expressed lexically or constructionally in other languages.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The predicate-initial verbless clause is the unmarked attribution pattern. The *sa totoo lang* and *ang totoo* discourse frames are highly grammaticalized sincerity and corrective markers. The *may/wala* + nominal existential construction (*may katotohanan*, *walang katotohanan*) is a distinctive pattern for asserting or denying the presence of truth in a claim. The *totoo na* construction (with change-of-state particle *na*) is a distinctive inchoative for marking that something previously doubted has been confirmed.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *totoo/kasinungalingan* and *tunay/huwad* pairs are the primary lexical oppositions. The *may katotohanan/walang katotohanan* constructional pair is distinctive in using the existential frame rather than a copular negation. The *tama/mali* pair is the primary correctness opposition. The *tapat* root covers both the honesty/dishonesty and loyalty/disloyalty dimensions, creating a semantic overlap not present in most other languages.

### 2.7 Swahili (sw)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data distinguishes: (1) propositional truth (*kweli*, *ukweli*); (2) accuracy and correctness (*sahihi*, *usahihi*); (3) genuineness of objects (*halisi*, *uhalisi* vs. *bandia*, *ghushi*); (4) legal legitimacy (*halali*, *uhalali* vs. *haramu*); (5) reliability and trustworthiness (*uaminifu*, *amini*, *mwaminifu*); (6) certainty and doubt (*uhakika*, *hakika* vs. *shaka*); and (7) deception (*uongo*, *udanganyifu*, *kudanganya*). The Arabic loanword stratum is pervasive: *sahihi*, *halisi*, *halali*, *haramu*, *hakika*, *amini*, *shahidi*, *ushahidi* are all Arabic-derived. The *halali/haramu* pair carries both Islamic legal and broader secular evaluative meanings.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *u-* prefix is the primary abstract nominalizer (*ukweli*, *uhalisi*, *uaminifu*, *udanganyifu*). The *-sha/-isha* causative suffix is productive (*kuthibitisha*, *kuhakikisha*, *kusahihisha*, *kuhalalisha*). The *-ika/-eka* stative/inchoative suffix is productive and semantically distinct from the *-wa* passive (*kudanganyika* vs. *kudanganywa*). The *m-/wa-* agentive prefix is productive for negative-pole agents (*mwongo*, *mdanganyifu*) but the positive-pole "truth-teller" requires periphrasis (*mtu wa kweli*). The *piga uongo* (light verb + *uongo*) construction for lying has no parallel *piga kweli* construction for truth-telling.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The *ni/si* copular pair is the primary attribution/negation pattern. The *kwa kweli* adverbial frame is a grammaticalized sincerity marker. The *ukweli ni kwamba* frame is a standard corrective/clarifying construction. The *-ika* inchoative is the primary construction for agentless truth-revelation (*ulidhihirika*). The *nina/sina uhakika* possessive epistemic construction is the standard formula for expressing certainty and uncertainty.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *kweli/uongo* and *halisi/bandia* pairs are the primary lexical oppositions. The *halali/haramu* pair is a distinctive lexical opposition in the legal-religious domain. The *kudanganywa/kudanganyika* morphological pair is semantically significant in distinguishing agentive passive from inchoative. The *ni kweli/si kweli* constructional pair is the primary attribution/negation pair.

### 2.8 Quechua, Southern (qu)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data distinguishes: (1) truth and genuineness (*cheqa*, *cheqaq*); (2) correctness and straightness (*chiqan*, *allin*); (3) clarity and explicitness (*sut'i*); (4) error and mistake (*pantay*, *pantasqa*); (5) deception and lying (*llulla*, *llullakuy*, *llullaq*); (6) identity and sameness (*kikin*); (7) resemblance (*hina*); and (8) belief and trust (*iñiy*, *iñinapaq*). The *cheqa* root is the most productive and covers both propositional truth and genuineness of persons and objects. The *allin* root covers both moral goodness and practical correctness. The evidentiality system (*-m/-mi*, *-s/-si*, *-chá*) grammaticalizes distinctions between direct knowledge, reported information, and conjecture that are expressed lexically or constructionally in other languages.

**Derivational and morphological asymmetries:**
The *-ncha-* causative verbalizer is the primary transitive derivational pathway for adjectival roots (*cheqanchay*, *allinchay*, *sut'inchay*), while *-chi-* is used for verbal roots (*pantachiy*, *llullachiy*). The *-ka-* intransitive verbalizer is the primary inchoative pathway (*cheqakay*, *allinkay*). The *-q* agentive nominalizer is productive for negative-pole agents (*llullaq*, *pantaq*) but the positive-pole *cheqaq* functions primarily as an adjective rather than a person-characterization. The *-puni* emphatic suffix and *-lla* limitative suffix are productive across truth-domain items. No BECOME form is attested for *llulla*, creating an asymmetry with *cheqa* and *allin*.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The predicate-initial verbless clause with obligatory evidential enclitic is the unmarked attribution pattern. The *mana … -chu* frame is the standard negation pattern. The *[X kasqanta] yachay* nominalized subordinate clause is the standard construction for propositional knowledge. The *cheqanta rimanayki tiyan* deontic periphrasis is the standard construction for expressing obligation. The *ama llulla, ama suwa, ama qella* prohibitive triad is a culturally fixed formula.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *cheqa/llulla* pair is the foundational lexical opposition. The *cheqam/mana cheqachu* constructional pair is the primary attribution/negation pair. The three-way evidential opposition (*-m/-mi* vs. *-s/-si* vs. *-chá*) is a grammaticalized system with no direct parallel in other languages in the corpus. The *cheqanchay/cheqakay* morphological pair encodes the transitive/intransitive distinction within the same root family.

## 3. Cross-Language Summary

### 3.1 Recurring Convergences (patterns observed across many languages)

- **A primary binary opposition between truth and falsehood is present in all eight languages**, expressed through a lexical pair: zh 真/假, he *ʾemet/sheqer*, sa *satya/asatya*, el *αληθής/ψευδής*, en *true/false*, tl *totoo/kasinungalingan*, sw *kweli/uongo*, qu *cheqa/llulla*. In all languages, this pair is the foundational evaluative axis of the domain, and both poles participate in the same construction types (predication, modification, nominalization).

- **All eight languages distinguish at least two sub-domains within the truth-evaluation field**: (a) the truth or falsity of *statements and propositions*, and (b) the genuineness or inauthenticity of *objects, persons, or documents*. These two sub-domains are covered by overlapping but distinct vocabulary in every language (e.g., zh 真实 vs. 真伪; he *ʾemet* vs. *mezuyaf*; sa *satya* vs. *mithyā*; el *αληθής* vs. *πλαστός*; en *true* vs. *fake*; tl *totoo* vs. *huwad/peke*; sw *kweli* vs. *bandia*; qu *cheqa* vs. *llulla*).

- **Abstract nominalization of truth-domain adjectives is productive in all eight languages**, using language-specific suffixes: zh *-性* (*真实性*, *可靠性*); he *-ut* (*ʾaminut*, *neʾemanut*); sa *-tā/-tva* (*satyatā*, *mithyātva*); el *-ότητα* (*αυθεντικότητα*, *εγκυρότητα*); en *-ity/-ness* (*authenticity*, *truthfulness*); tl *ka-…-an* (*katotohanan*, *katapatan*); sw *u-* (*ukweli*, *uaminifu*); qu *-kay/-nchay* (*cheqakay*, *cheqanchay*). In all languages, these nominalizations are used in formal, legal, and philosophical registers.

- **Agentive nominalization shows a consistent asymmetry across languages**: negative-pole agents (liars, deceivers, forgers) are more consistently lexicalized as single words than positive-pole agents (truth-tellers). This pattern is explicitly documented in zh (*伪造者*, *欺骗者* but no *-者* form for truth-teller), he (*shaqran* "liar" but no *-an* agentive for truth-teller), el (*ψεύτης* "liar" but no lexicalized "truth-teller"), en (*faker*, *counterfeiter* but *truth-teller* requires a compound), tl (*sinungaling* "liar" but no parallel agentive for honest person), sw (*mwongo*, *mdanganyifu* but *mtu wa kweli* requires periphrasis), and qu (*llullaq* "liar" but *cheqaq* functions primarily as adjective).

- **Discourse-framing constructions for introducing frank or corrective statements are attested in all eight languages**, though their forms vary: zh *实际上*, *事实上*; he *ha-ʾemet hi she-*; sa *vastutaḥ*, *tattvataḥ*; el *η αλήθεια είναι ότι*; en *to tell the truth*, *truth be told*; tl *sa totoo lang*, *ang totoo*; sw *kwa kweli*, *ukweli ni kwamba*; qu *cheqaqta rimay*. In all languages, these constructions signal that the speaker is about to state what is actually the case, often in contrast to a prior claim or expectation.

- **Causative constructions for the act of verifying, confirming, or correcting are attested in all eight languages**: zh *核实*, *鉴定*; he *leʾammet*, *letaqqef*; sa *satyāpana*, *pramāṇīkaraṇa*; el *επαληθεύω*, *αποδεικνύω*; en *verify*, *authenticate*, *validate*; tl *patunayan*, *cheqanchay*; sw *kuthibitisha*, *kuhakikisha*; qu *cheqanchay*, *cheqachiy*. In all languages, these causative forms are more common in formal, legal, and administrative registers than in everyday speech.

- **Proverbial or semi-fixed expressions asserting that truth is painful, that truth endures, or that truth will eventually be revealed are attested in at least six of the eight languages**: zh *真金不怕火炼*; he *ʾemet marah* (bitter truth); el *η αλήθεια πονάει*, *η αλήθεια βγαίνει πάντα στο φως*; en *the truth hurts*, *the truth will out*; tl *ang katotohanan ay masakit*; sw *ukweli unauma*, *kweli haiozi*; qu (no direct parallel documented). This pattern is absent or not documented for sa and qu.

---

### 3.2 Major Divergences (strong differences between languages)

- **Grammaticalized evidentiality is present only in Quechua (qu)** among the eight languages. The three-way distinction between direct knowledge (*-m/-mi*), reported information (*-s/-si*), and conjecture (*-chá*) is obligatorily marked on predicates and is a grammatical feature of the language rather than a lexical or constructional choice. In all other languages, the source of knowledge is expressed lexically (e.g., en *reportedly*, *allegedly*; tl *daw*; sw *-s/-si* is not grammaticalized in the same way) or through specific constructions, but not as an obligatory grammatical category.

- **The ontological dimension of truth (what genuinely exists vs. what is unreal) is most elaborately developed in Sanskrit (sa)**, where the *sat/asat* opposition, the *mithyā* category, and the *paramārtha/vyāvahārika* distinction constitute a distinct semantic group not paralleled in the other languages. While other languages have terms for "real" vs. "unreal" (zh 真实/虚假; el *αληθινός/φαινομενικός*; en *real/illusory*), only sa develops a multi-level ontological framework with named intermediate categories (*mithyā* as neither real nor unreal) and named levels of analysis (*paramārtha*, *vyāvahārika*, *pratibhāsa*).

- **The legal-religious legitimacy dimension (*halal/haram*) is most prominently developed in Swahili (sw) and Hebrew (he)**, reflecting the influence of Arabic and Islamic legal vocabulary. The *halali/haramu* pair in sw and the *kasher/pasul* pair in he combine ritual fitness with legal admissibility in ways that have no direct parallel in the other six languages. In other languages, legal validity is expressed through separate vocabulary (zh 合法/违法; el *έγκυρος/άκυρος*; en *valid/invalid*) without the religious-legal fusion characteristic of these two languages.

- **The *loob* (inner self) constructions in Tagalog (tl)** — *tapat na loob*, *katapatan ng loob*, *tapat ang kanyang loob* — locate moral evaluation in a culturally specific concept of the inner self that has no direct parallel in the other seven languages. While other languages have terms for sincerity and inner honesty (zh 真诚, 真心; he *kanut*; en *sincere*; qu *cheqa sonqo*), the *loob* constructions in tl are distinctive in their cultural specificity and their role in the moral-psychological framework of Tagalog discourse.

- **The *ṛta* (cosmic order) dimension in Sanskrit (sa)** — covering the ordered functioning of the cosmos and the moral-ritual rightness aligned with it — has no parallel in the other seven languages. While other languages have terms for moral rightness (zh 道德; he *tsedeq*; en *right*; tl *tama*; sw *haki*; qu *allin*), only sa develops a cosmological framework in which truth and cosmic order are aspects of the same concept (*ṛta*), with the *ṛta/anṛta* opposition predating and partially overlapping with the *satya/asatya* opposition.

- **The *post-truth* compound (en *post-truth*, el *μετα-αλήθεια*, zh 后真相 [implied but not explicitly documented])** is documented as a recent formation in English and Greek, reflecting a contemporary epistemic discourse that is not documented in the other six languages in the corpus. This is a single-language or two-language feature in the data as presented.

- **The distinction between *accurate* (tolerates a specified margin) and *exact* (no deviation)** is explicitly documented as a lexical contrast in English (en) and is paralleled in Hebrew (*meduyaq* vs. *meshuʿar*) and Chinese (*准确* vs. *精确* [implied]), but is not explicitly documented as a distinct lexical contrast in Tagalog, Swahili, or Quechua in the available data.

---

### 3.3 Asymmetries, Gaps, and Irregularities

- **The *-ncha-* causative verbalizer in Quechua (qu) applies to adjectival roots (*cheqa*, *allin*, *sut'i*) but not to the negative root *llulla***, which instead uses *-chi-* directly. This asymmetry — different causative pathways for positive and negative evaluative roots — is documented in the data and has no direct parallel in the other languages, where causative formation is typically uniform across evaluative polarity.

- **The *ʾi-* negation prefix in Hebrew (he) applies productively to *-ut* nominalizations** (*ʾi-diyyuq*, *ʾi-sevirut*, *ʾi-ḥuqiyyut*) but not to the corresponding adjectives, which use *lo* or *bilti* instead. This creates an asymmetry between the adjectival and nominalized negation systems that is not paralleled in the other languages, where negation strategies tend to be more uniform across word classes.

- **The *piga uongo* (light verb + *uongo*) construction for lying in Swahili (sw) has no parallel *piga kweli* construction for truth-telling**, which instead uses *sema ukweli* (a different light verb). This asymmetry — different light verbs for the positive and negative poles of the same domain — is explicitly documented in the data and is not paralleled in the other languages.

- **The *kasher/pasul* pair in Hebrew (he) is a lexical opposition formed from two unrelated roots** (not a morphological negation), while most other language pairs in this domain are formed by prefixal negation of a single root. This makes *kasher/pasul* structurally parallel to zh 合法/违法 and sw *halali/haramu* (lexical oppositions) rather than to he *ʾamin/lo ʾamin* or en *valid/invalid* (morphological negations).

- **The *mithyā* category in Sanskrit (sa) disrupts the binary *sat/asat* opposition** by introducing a third ontological value (neither real nor unreal) specific to Advaita Vedānta. | Group 1 — Expressions used to evaluate whether a statement or claim is correct or true | These expressions are used in everyday spoken Hebrew and in journalistic and analytical writing to confirm or deny that a statement, answer, or fact is correct. | Cognition-evaluating terms in epistemological argument | These terms are used in Sanskrit philosophical literature — primarily Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Buddhist epistemology — to assess whether a given cognitive episode accurately apprehends the object it is directed at. They appear in technical discussions of the structure of knowledge, the causes of error, and the distinction between reliable and unreliable cognitive episodes. They are regularly contrasted with one another as positive and negative poles of the same evaluative dimension. | प्रमा / *pramā*; अप्रमा / *apramā*; यथार्थज्ञान / *yathārthajñāna*; भ्रम / *bhrama*; विपर्यय / *viparyaya*; भ्रमज्ञान / *bhramajñāna*; मिथ्याज्ञान / *mithyājñāna*; भ्रमो न प्रमा / *bhramo na pramā*; विपर्ययो न प्रमा / *viparyayo na pramā*; भ्रान्ति / *bhrānti*; भ्रान्त / *bhrānta*; भ्रान्तिज्ञान / *bhrānti-jñāna*; भ्रामक / *bhrāmaka*; विपर्यस्त / *viparyasta*; मिथ्यादृष्टि / *mithyā-dṛṣṭi*; अविसंवादिन् / *avisaṃvādin*; असत्ख्याति / *asatkhyāti*; विपर्ययो मिथ्याज्ञानम् / *viparyayo mithyājñānam*; मिथ्याज्ञानं निवर्तते सम्यग्ज्ञानेन / *mithyājñānaṃ nivartate samyag-jñānena*; रज्जौ सर्पभ्रान्तिः / *rajjau sarpa-bhrāntiḥ*; भ्रान्तिः निवर्तते / *bhrāntiḥ nivartate*; बाधेन भ्रान्तिः निवर्तते / *bādhena bhrāntiḥ nivartate*; बाधित / *bādhita*; बाधा / *bādhā* | मिथ्याज्ञान / *mithyājñāna* (also Group 5, carries Advaita Vedānta ontological connotations); भ्रम / *bhrama* and विपर्यय / *viparyaya* (near-synonyms across different school vocabularies); भ्रान्ति / *bhrānti* (near-synonym of *bhrama*) | *Bhrama* and *viparyaya* are near-synonyms in function but belong to different school vocabularies; *bhrama* is the standard Nyāya term, *viparyaya* the standard Sāṃkhya-Yoga term. *Bhrānti* is a near-synonym of *bhrama* emphasizing the state of being in error. *Mithyājñāna* carries additional Advaita Vedānta connotations about the ontological status of the object, not only the accuracy of the cognition. *Apramā* is the most technically neutral negation. *Avisaṃvādin* is a Buddhist *pramāṇa*-theory term. |
| Source-evaluating terms in epistemological argument | These terms are used to assess not the cognition itself but the means, source, or procedure by which it is produced. They appear in debates across all major Sanskrit philosophical schools about which sources of knowledge count as authoritative and why. The central question is not whether a particular cognition is accurate but whether the *means* by which it was arrived at is reliable. The central term *pramāṇa* generates a large cluster of derived expressions that evaluate sources as genuine, spurious, absent, or contested. | प्रमाण / *pramāṇa*; प्रामाण्य / *prāmāṇya*; अप्रामाण्य / *aprāmāṇya*; स्वतःप्रामाण्य / *svataḥprāmāṇya*; परतःप्रामाण्य / *parataḥprāmāṇya*; प्रमाणाभास / *pramāṇābhāsa*; हेत्वाभास / *hetvābhāsa*; प्रमाणेन सिद्धम् / *pramāṇena siddham*; प्रमाणाभावात् / *pramāṇābhāvāt*; प्रमाणं नास्ति / *pramāṇaṃ nāsti*; प्रमाणविरुद्ध / *pramāṇaviruddha*; प्रमाणसिद्ध / *pramāṇasiddha*; अनुमान / *anumāna*; अनुमिति / *anumiti*; उपमान / *upamāna*; प्रामाणिक / *prāmāṇika*; अप्रमाण / *apramāṇa*; अप्रामाणिक / *aprāmāṇika*; प्रमाणभूत / *pramāṇabhūta*; प्रमाणता / *pramāṇatā*; प्रमातृ / *pramātṛ*; प्रमेय / *prameya*; वेदः प्रमाणम् / *vedaḥ pramāṇam*; प्रमाणं किम्? / *pramāṇaṃ kim?*; न तत्र प्रमाणम् अस्ति / *na tatra pramāṇam asti*; प्रमायाः करणं प्रमाणम् / *pramāyāḥ karaṇaṃ pramāṇam*; हेत्वाभासो न हेतुः / *hetvābhāso na hetuḥ* | प्रमाण / *pramāṇa* (also Group 1, as the source that produces *pramā*); हेत्वाभास / *hetvābhāsa* (a specific application of the *ābhāsa* pattern to inferential reasoning) | The *svataḥ/parataḥ* pair marks a specific intra-school debate about the locus of validity-conferring conditions. *Hetvābhāsa* is a specialized application of the *ābhāsa* (semblance) pattern to the specific case of inferential reasoning. *Pramāṇābhāsa* is the more general term for spurious epistemic sources. This group is closely related to Group 1 but is distinct: Group 1 terms evaluate individual cognitions or statements, while Group 2 terms evaluate the *sources and methods* that generate cognitions. The two groups interact: a cognition is *pramā* (Group 1) when it results from a *pramāṇa* (Group 2). |
| Speech-evaluating terms in ethical and legal contexts | These terms are used in Dharmaśāstra, epic literature, and legal contexts to evaluate utterances, testimony, and speech acts as truthful, false, or wrongful. The evaluative dimension here is primarily moral and legal rather than epistemological. | सत्य / *satya*; असत्य / *asatya*; अनृत / *anṛta*; तथ्य / *tathya*; सत्यवादिन् / *satyavādin*; असत्यवादिन् / *asatyavādin*; मिथ्यावादिन् / *mithyāvādin*; सत्यवचन / *satyavacana*; असत्यवचन / *asatyavacana*; अनृतवचन / *anṛtavacana*; असत्यभाषण / *asatya-bhāṣaṇa*; अनृतभाषिन् / *anṛta-bhāṣin*; सत्यवाक्य / *satya-vākya*; सत्यसंध / *satyasaṃdha*; सत्यं वद / *satyaṃ vada*; सत्यं ब्रूयात् / *satyaṃ brūyāt*; असत्यं न वदेत् / *asatyaṃ na vadet*; अनृतं न वदेत् / *anṛtaṃ na vadet*; तथ्यं वदति / *tathyaṃ vadati*; असत्यं पापम् / *asatyaṃ pāpam*; असत्यं वदति / *asatyaṃ vadati*; मिथ्या न वदेत् / *mithyā na vadet*; सत्यं नास्ति परो धर्मः / *satyaṃ nāsti paro dharmaḥ*; सत्यं परं धर्मः / *satyaṃ paraṃ dharmaḥ* | सत्य / *satya* (also Groups 4, 5, 6); अनृत / *anṛta* (older Vedic term with cosmological connotations, overlapping with Group 5); तथ्य / *tathya* (also Group 4); मिथ्यावादिन् / *mithyāvādin* (overlapping with Group 1) | *Satya* and *asatya* are the most widely used pair in post-Vedic prose. *Anṛta* is the older Vedic term and carries cosmological connotations that *asatya* does not. *Tathya* is more restricted to factual accuracy in legal and narrative contexts and lacks the moral weight of *satya*. | Reality-correspondence terms in philosophical and general prose | These terms are used to assess whether a description, property, or characterization pertains to how things actually are, as opposed to how they appear, are conventionally described, or are merely named. They appear in philosophical argument when distinguishing genuine from apparent or conventional properties, and in general prose when asserting that an account is accurate to the facts. They are regularly contrasted with terms for appearance, convention, or mere verbal designation. | वास्तव / *vāstava*; वस्तु / *vastu*; यथार्थ / *yathārtha*; तथ्य / *tathya*; वस्तुतः / *vastutaḥ*; वास्तवतः / *vāstavataḥ*; वस्तुस्थिति / *vastusthiti*; वस्तुनि यथावत् ज्ञानम् / *vastuni yathāvat jñānam*; वस्तु न शब्दाधीनम् / *vastu na śabdādhīnam*; वस्तुबलात् / *vastubalaāt*; वास्तविक / *vāstavika*; वस्तुस्वभाव / *vastusvabhāva*; वस्तुतन्त्र / *vastu-tantra*; वस्तुसत् / *vastu-sat*; यथार्थता / *yathārthatā*; आभासमात्रम् न वस्तु / *ābhāsamātram na vastu* | वस्तु / *vastu* (also Group 5); यथार्थ / *yathārtha* (also Group 1); तथ्य / *tathya* (also Group 3) | *Vastu* and *vāstava* are closely related, with *vastu* being the noun (the real thing) and *vāstava* the adjective (pertaining to the real thing). *Yathārtha* emphasizes the correspondence relation between a description and its object, while *vastu*/*vāstava* emphasize the ontological status of the object itself. *Tathya* overlaps with this group but is more restricted to factual accuracy in testimony and narrative. |

In moral contexts it can indicate rightness of action. | [CORE] |
| σωστός | sostós | from σώζω (to save, preserve); "preserved intact," hence "correct, sound" | correct, right, proper, accurate, sound | The most common colloquial term for "correct" in modern Greek, used of answers, behavior, persons, procedures, and objects. Overlaps with ορθός but is more frequent in informal registers. Η σωστή απάντηση means "the correct answer." | [CORE] |
| λανθασμένος | lanthazmenos | past participle of λανθάνομαι (to be mistaken, to err) | wrong, mistaken, erroneous, incorrect | Applied to beliefs, statements, calculations, and actions to indicate that they are in error. Common in everyday and educational contexts as the standard antonym of σωστός. | [CORE] |
| έγκυρος | éngiros | from ἐν- (in) + κῦρος (authority, validity); "having authority" | valid, authoritative, reliable, credible, legitimate | Used in legal, administrative, and epistemic contexts to indicate that a document, argument, decision, or source carries recognized authority or meets formal requirements. A passport, contract, or election may be described as έγκυρος. Contrasts with άκυρος ("invalid, null"). Έγκυρο συμβόλαιο means "valid contract." | [CORE] |
| νόμιμος | nómimos | from νόμος (law); "according to law" | legal, lawful, legitimate | Indicates conformity with legal norms or established rules. Applied to persons, actions, and documents. Contrasts with παράνομος (illegal). | [CORE] |
| αξιόπιστος | aksiópistos | ἄξιος (worthy) + πίστις (trust, faith); "worthy of trust" | reliable, trustworthy, credible | Applied to persons, sources, institutions, and testimonies to indicate that they merit confidence and can be trusted or believed. Frequently used in journalistic and legal contexts when evaluating the credibility of witnesses or information sources. Αξιόπιστη πηγή means "reliable source." | [CORE] |
| αναξιόπιστος | anaksiópistos | privative ἀν- + αξιόπιστος; "not worthy of trust" | unreliable, untrustworthy, incredible | The direct negation of αξιόπιστος, applied to persons, sources, and claims. Used in evaluative contexts where credibility is at issue. | [CORE] |
| αξιόλογος | aksiólogos | ἄξιος (worthy) + λόγος (word, account, reason); "worthy of account" | noteworthy, significant, considerable, creditable, of merit | Used to evaluate persons, achievements, or works as deserving recognition or serious consideration. Applied to persons, works, or achievements to indicate that they are genuinely worthy of attention or merit. Carries a positive evaluative force and appears in both formal and informal registers, as well as academic and critical registers. | [CORE] |
| νόθος | nóthos | "of illegitimate birth," hence "spurious, counterfeit" | spurious, illegitimate, counterfeit, false, adulterated | Historically used of illegitimate children; extended to texts, documents, and objects to indicate that they are not what they claim to be. Used in philological and legal contexts (e.g., a νόθο κείμενο is a text of doubtful authenticity). In textual criticism, applied to works falsely attributed to an author. | [CORE] |
| πλαστός | plastós | from πλάσσω / πλάθω (to mold, fabricate); "fabricated, molded" | forged, counterfeit, fake, fabricated | Applied to documents, signatures, currency, and identities to indicate deliberate falsification. Implies deliberate fabrication. Πλαστή ταυτότητα is a forged identity document; πλαστό διαβατήριο means "forged passport." Commonly used in legal and criminal contexts. | [CORE] |
| ψεύτικος | psévtikos / pséftikos | from ψεύτης (liar) / ψεύδος (falsehood, lie); "of the nature of a lie, false" | false, fake, counterfeit, lying | A common colloquial adjective applied to objects, persons, and statements to indicate that they are not genuine or truthful. Less formal than πλαστός and broader in application. Contrasts with αληθινός and γνήσιος in everyday speech. | [CORE] |
| ψευδής | psevdís | from ψεύδος (falsehood); "characterized by falsehood" | false, untrue, mendacious, lying, spurious | More formal than ψεύτικος; used of statements, testimony, documents, and representations in legal and philosophical contexts to indicate falsity or deceptiveness. A ψευδής κατάθεση is false testimony. Participates in compounds such as ψευδώνυμο (pseudonym). | [CORE] |
| ψεύδος | psévdos | "falsehood, lie" | falsehood, lie, untruth | The primary noun for a falsehood or lie, used in philosophical, legal, and everyday contexts. Participates in a large derivational family: ψεύτης (liar), ψεύδομαι (to lie), ψευδής (false). Also appears in the compound ψευδώνυμο and in compounds such as ψευδοεπιστήμη ("pseudoscience"). In everyday speech the plural ψέματα is the colloquial form (λέω ψέματα, "I tell lies"). | [CORE] |
| αμφίβολος | amfívolos | ἀμφί (on both sides) + βάλλω (to throw); "thrown both ways, doubtful" | doubtful, dubious, questionable, ambiguous | Applied to persons, situations, claims, and cases whose reliability, truth, or quality is in question or uncertain. An αμφίβολη υπόθεση is a dubious case or affair. Used in both everyday and formal registers. | [CORE] |
| αμφισβητήσιμος | amfisvitiísimos | from αμφισβητώ (to dispute, contest); "disputable, contestable" | disputable, contestable, questionable, debatable | Applied to claims, titles, rights, and facts that are open to challenge or have not been definitively established. More formal than αμφίβολος and more specifically tied to the possibility of active contestation. Frequently used in legal and academic contexts to flag that a proposition or right is not settled. | [CORE] |
| αμφισβητώ | amfisviтó | ἀμφί (on both sides) + σβητός; conventionally "to dispute, contest" | to dispute, to contest, to challenge, to question | A verb used to indicate that a claim, right, or fact is being actively challenged. Used in legal proceedings (αμφισβητώ μια κατάθεση) and in everyday argument. Productive derivational base for αμφισβήτηση, αμφισβητήσιμος. | [CORE] |
| αδιαμφισβήτητος | adiamfisvitiitos | ἀ- (privative) + διαμφισβητέω (to dispute thoroughly); "not disputable" | indisputable, unquestionable, undeniable | Applied to facts, rights, and truths that are held to be beyond reasonable challenge. Used for emphasis in legal, rhetorical, and everyday contexts. | [CORE] |
| αποδεδειγμένος | apodedeignménos | perfect passive participle of ἀποδείκνυμι (to demonstrate, prove); "having been demonstrated" | proven, demonstrated, established | Applied to facts, claims, and propositions that have been shown to be true through evidence or argument. Used in legal, scientific, and everyday contexts. | [CORE] |
| τεκμηριωμένος | tekmirio̱ménos | from τεκμήριον (evidence, proof); "supported by evidence" | documented, evidenced, substantiated | Applied to claims, arguments, and positions that are backed by concrete evidence or documentation. Common in journalistic, academic, and legal registers. | [CORE] |
| επαληθεύω | epalithévo | ἐπί (upon, toward) + αληθεύω (to be true); "to verify, confirm as true" | to verify, to confirm, to validate, to corroborate | Used in scientific, journalistic, and administrative contexts to indicate the process of checking whether a claim, result, or document is accurate or genuine. The noun επαλήθευση is used for the act of verification. | [CORE] |
| επαλήθευση | epalíthefsi | nominal form of επαληθεύω; "the act of verifying" | verification, confirmation, validation | Used in scientific, legal, and administrative contexts to refer to the process or result of checking accuracy or truth. Appears in formal documents and procedures. | [CORE] |
| διαψεύδω | diapsévdo | διά (through, thoroughly) + ψεύδω (to deceive, to falsify); "to refute, to give the lie to" | to refute, to deny, to disprove, to contradict | Used when a claim, rumor, or allegation is officially or demonstrably shown to be false. Common in journalistic and official contexts (e.g., η κυβέρνηση διέψευσε τις φήμες, "the government denied/refuted the rumors"). | [CORE] |
| διαπίστωση | diapístoси | from διαπιστώνω (to ascertain, establish); "the act of ascertaining" | finding, ascertainment, determination, observation | Used to refer to the result of an investigation or observation that establishes a fact. Common in official reports, medical contexts, and everyday speech when someone states what they have found to be the case. | [CORE] |
| τεκμήριο | tekmírio | from τεκμαίρομαι (to infer, judge by signs); "sign, proof, evidence" | evidence, proof, indication, token | Used in legal and argumentative contexts to refer to a piece of evidence or an indicator that supports a conclusion. A τεκμήριο is typically indirect evidence from which a fact is inferred, distinguishing it from direct proof. | [CORE] |
| απόδειξη | apódhiksi | from αποδεικνύω (to demonstrate, prove); "demonstration, proof" | proof, evidence, receipt, demonstration | Used in logical, legal, and everyday contexts to refer to something that proves or demonstrates a claim. In commercial contexts it also means "receipt." The dual usage reflects the general sense of something that establishes a fact. | [CORE] |
| εικονικός | eikonikós / ikonikós | from εικόνα / εἰκών (image, icon); "of or like an image" | simulated, virtual, nominal, figurative; also: iconic | In modern usage, applied to simulated or nominal states of affairs (e.g., εικονική πραγματικότητα = virtual reality). Can also mean "nominal" or "token" in legal and financial contexts, indicating something that resembles but is not the real thing. In legal contexts, an εικονική πράξη is a sham transaction. The evaluative force is that something appears to be what it is not. | [CORE] |
| φαινομενικός | fenomenikós | from φαινόμενον (that which appears); "of or pertaining to appearance" | apparent, seeming, ostensible | Applied to qualities or states that appear to be the case but may not correspond to underlying reality. Φαινομενική επιτυχία means "apparent success." | [CORE] |
| ουσιαστικός | usiástikos / ussiastikós | from οὐσία (essence, substance, being); "of or pertaining to essence" | essential, substantive, real, fundamental, material | Used to distinguish what is genuinely or fundamentally the case from what is merely formal or superficial. In legal contexts, ουσιαστικό δίκαιο means "substantive law" as opposed to procedural law. Also used in everyday speech to mean "real" or "meaningful." Ουσιαστική διαφορά means "a substantive difference." | [CORE] |
| ουσία | ussía | from εἶναι (to be); "being, essence, substance" | essence, substance, matter, gist | Used in philosophical contexts for the fundamental nature of a thing, and in everyday contexts for the essential point or substance of a matter (e.g., η ουσία του ζητήματος, "the substance/gist of the matter"). Also used in legal contexts for "substance" as opposed to form. | [CORE] |
| τυπικός | tipikós | from τύπος (type, form, stamp); "of or pertaining to form or type" | formal, nominal, typical, perfunctory | Often used in contrast to ουσιαστικός to indicate that something satisfies formal requirements without genuine substance. Τυπική συμμόρφωση means "formal compliance." | [CORE] |
| κατ' ουσίαν | kat' usían | κατά (according to, in respect of) + οὐσία (essence); "in respect of essence" | essentially, substantially, in substance | A fixed prepositional expression used to indicate that something is true or the case at the level of substance or essence, as opposed to mere form. Common in legal and philosophical discourse. | [CORE] |
| ομοιότητα | omióтita | from όμοιος (similar, like); "likeness, resemblance" | resemblance, similarity, likeness | Used to describe the degree to which one thing resembles another, relevant in aesthetic evaluation (resemblance of a portrait to its subject) and in legal contexts (resemblance of a trademark to another). Participates in evaluative judgments about representation. | [CORE] |
| αντίγραφο | andígrafo | ἀντί (against, in place of) + γράφω (to write); "written in place of" | copy, reproduction, transcript | Used of documents, artworks, and files to indicate that something is a reproduction rather than the original. The distinction between αντίγραφο and πρωτότυπο (original) is central to legal and archival evaluation of authenticity. | [CORE] |
| πρωτότυπο | protótipo | πρῶτος (first) + τύπος (type, impression); "first impression, original" | original, prototype | Used to designate the original version of a document, artwork, or text as opposed to copies or translations. In aesthetic and legal contexts, the πρωτότυπο carries special authority or value. | [CORE] |
| παραποίηση | parapiísi | from παραποιώ (to alter, falsify); "alteration, falsification" | falsification, adulteration, distortion, tampering | Used in legal and everyday contexts to refer to the deliberate alteration of a document, substance, or account so as to misrepresent it. A παραποίηση εγγράφου is the falsification of a document, a criminal offense. | [CORE] |
| δήθεν | díthен | from δή (indeed, just) + θεν (suffix of origin/manner); "supposedly, allegedly" | supposedly, allegedly, so-called, ostensibly | A particle or adverb expressing skepticism or irony about a claim — that something is presented as being the case but the speaker doubts it. Frequently used with scare-quote force in everyday speech. | [CORE] |
| τάχα | tácha | originally "quickly, perhaps"; in modern usage, "supposedly, as if" | supposedly, allegedly, as if, ostensibly | Used colloquially to cast doubt on a claim or to indicate that something is presented as true but is not believed by the speaker. Often interchangeable with δήθεν in informal registers, though with slightly different pragmatic nuances. | [CORE] |
| φερόμενος ως | ferómenos os | present participle of φέρω (to carry, bear) + ως (as); "being carried/presented as" | alleged, purported, so-called, presented as | A fixed participial expression used in legal, journalistic, and formal contexts to indicate that something is described or presented as having a certain identity or status without that status being confirmed (e.g., φερόμενος ως ιδιοκτήτης, "the purported owner"). | [CORE] |
| κατά φαινόμενον | katá fenómenon | κατά (according to) + φαινόμενον (appearance); "according to appearance" | apparently, ostensibly, in appearance | A fixed prepositional expression contrasting with κατ' ουσίαν, used to indicate that something holds only at the level of appearance. Found in philosophical and formal registers. | [MARGINAL] |
| εικαζόμενος | eikazómenos / ikazómenos | present passive participle of εἰκάζω (to conjecture, liken); "conjectured, supposed" | alleged, supposed, presumed, putative, conjectured | Used in legal and journalistic contexts to describe a person or fact whose status has not been established (e.g., ο εικαζόμενος δράστης, "the alleged perpetrator"). Marks epistemic reservation about a claim. | [MARGINAL] |
| εικός | ikós | from ἔοικα (to seem, resemble); "that which seems likely, probable" | probable, likely, plausible, verisimilar | Found primarily in classical and formal philosophical registers to indicate what is probable or plausible as opposed to what is certain or demonstrated. Less common in contemporary everyday Greek but retained in set expressions and academic writing. | [MARGINAL] |
| αναληθής | analithís | ἀν- (privative) + αληθής; "not true" | untrue, false | A formal or literary negation of αληθής, used in philosophical and written contexts. Less common in everyday speech than ψευδής; tends to appear in contexts where the negation of truth-value is being discussed explicitly. | [MARGINAL] |
| κίβδηλος | kívdhilos / kívdilos | "adulterated, counterfeit" (of coins originally); "base, spurious" | counterfeit, spurious, base, debased, adulterated | Originally applied to debased or counterfeit coinage; extended metaphorically to persons, arguments, and values considered inauthentic or morally debased. Used in formal, literary, and philosophical registers to describe something that appears genuine but is not. Less common in everyday Modern Greek; more frequent in written and elevated registers than πλαστός or ψεύτικος. | [MARGINAL] |
| εικαστικός | eikastikós | from εικάζω (to represent by likeness, to conjecture); "of or pertaining to representation by likeness" | visual (arts), representational, figurative | In Modern Greek, primarily used in the fixed expression εικαστικές τέχνες ("visual/plastic arts"), referring to arts that produce visible representations. The term carries the sense of arts concerned with likeness and representation, though its evaluative dimension (resemblance, fidelity of representation) is more prominent in older or technical usage. | [MARGINAL] |
| αλήθεια (Root 1, anchor) | alíthia | αληθ- (truth) + -εια (abstract noun suffix); "the state of being unconcealed" | truth, truthfulness | The primary noun for truth in all registers. Already listed in P1; included here as the base form for the expansion. | [CORE] |
| αληθής (Root 1, anchor) | alithís | αληθ- (truth) + -ής (adjectival suffix) | true, truthful | Base adjective for truth-value; already in P1. Included as anchor form. | [CORE] |
| αληθινός (Root 1, anchor) | alithinós | αληθ- (truth) + -ινός (adjectival suffix indicating nature or material) | real, genuine, true | Already in P1. Included as anchor form. | [CORE] |
| αληθεύω | alithévo | αληθ- (truth) + -εύω (verbal suffix); "to be truthful, to tell the truth" | to speak the truth, to be truthful, to be accurate | Used in philosophical, literary, and formal registers to describe the act of telling the truth or being in a state of truthfulness. Less common in everyday speech than λέω την αλήθεια. Αληθεύει ότι… means "it is true that…" in formal writing. | [CORE] |
| επαληθεύω (Root 1) | epalithévo | επί (upon, further) + αληθ- (truth) + -εύω (verbal suffix) | to verify, to confirm, to validate | Already in P1. Included here as a derived verbal form. | [CORE] |
| επαλήθευση (Root 1) | epalíthefsi | επί + αληθ- + -ευση (verbal noun suffix) | verification, confirmation, validation | The noun corresponding to επαληθεύω. Used in scientific, administrative, journalistic, and legal contexts to refer to the process or act of verifying a claim, result, or document. | [CORE] |
| επαληθεύσιμος | epalithéfsimos | επαληθεύω (to verify) + -σιμος (adjectival suffix indicating possibility); "capable of being verified" | verifiable | Used in scientific, philosophical, and journalistic contexts to describe claims or hypotheses that can in principle be checked against evidence. Related to the concept of falsifiability in philosophy of science. | [CORE] |
| αληθοφανής | alithofanís | αληθο- (truth-) + φαίνομαι (to appear) + -ής (adjectival suffix); "appearing true" | verisimilar, plausible, lifelike, credible, truth-seeming | Applied to narratives, arguments, and representations that have the appearance of truth or reality without necessarily being true. Used in literary criticism, rhetoric, and philosophical discussion of probability, and in everyday evaluation of stories or claims. | [CORE] |
| αληθοφάνεια | alithofánia | αληθο- (truth-) + φαίνομαι (to appear) + -εια (abstract noun suffix); "the quality of appearing true" | verisimilitude, plausibility, appearance of truth | Used in literary criticism, rhetoric, and philosophy to describe the quality of appearing true or lifelike, without necessarily being true. Applied to narrative, argument, and representation. Corresponds to the classical concept of verisimilitude. Η αληθοφάνεια ενός μυθιστορήματος means "the verisimilitude of a novel." | [CORE] |
| αληθοφάνεια αφήγησης | alithofánia afígisis | αληθοφάνεια (verisimilitude) + αφήγηση (narration) | narrative verisimilitude | A fixed collocation used in literary theory and narratology to refer to the quality of a narrative that makes it seem true or realistic. Common in academic literary criticism and rhetoric. | [CORE] |
| αληθοφανής αφήγηση | alithofanís afígisi | αληθοφανής (verisimilar) + αφήγηση (narration) | verisimilar narrative, plausible account | Used in literary theory and narratology to describe a narrative that achieves the effect of reality or truth. Common in academic literary criticism and rhetoric. | [CORE] |
| αληθινά | alithiná | αληθινός (true, genuine) + -α (adverbial suffix); "truly, genuinely" | truly, really, genuinely | Common adverbial form used in everyday speech to intensify or affirm the truth of a statement. Also used as a discourse marker of sincerity. "Αληθινά δεν το ήξερα" = "I truly didn't know." | [CORE] |
| αληθώς | alithós | αληθ- (truth) + -ώς (adverbial suffix) | truly, verily, in truth | A formal or archaic adverb used in religious, liturgical, and elevated literary contexts. Appears in the Orthodox liturgical response Αληθώς ανέστη ("He is truly risen"). | [CORE] |
| Αληθώς ανέστη | Alithós anésti | αληθώς (truly) + ανέστη (he rose, aorist of ανίσταμαι) | He is truly risen | The liturgical response in the Greek Orthodox Easter service, spoken in reply to Χριστός ανέστη ("Christ is risen"). A fixed religious formula. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια (exclamative) | alíthia | αλήθεια (truth); used as a discourse particle | Really? / Truly? / By the way | Used as a conversational interjection to express surprise ("Αλήθεια;" = "Really?") or to introduce a new topic ("Αλήθεια, ήθελα να σε ρωτήσω…" = "By the way, I wanted to ask you…"). Extremely frequent in spoken Greek. | [CORE] |
| στ' αλήθεια | st' alíthia | εις (to/in) + τη (the) + αλήθεια (truth); "in truth" | truly, in truth, honestly, really | Fixed adverbial phrase used in everyday speech to intensify or affirm a statement, or to ask whether something is genuinely the case. "Στ' αλήθεια, δεν ξέρω τι να πω" = "Honestly, I don't know what to say." | [CORE] |
| η αλήθεια είναι ότι | i alíthia íne óti | η αλήθεια (the truth) + είναι (is) + ότι (that) | the truth is that… | A fixed clausal frame used to introduce a frank or corrective statement, often conceding something the speaker might prefer not to admit. Functions to signal that what follows is the speaker's genuine assessment, often contrasting with a previous claim or expectation. Extremely common in both spoken and written Greek. | [CORE] |
| λέω την αλήθεια | léo tin alíthia | λέω (I say) + την αλήθεια (the truth) | to tell the truth | The standard colloquial expression for telling the truth. Used in everyday speech, legal contexts (witness testimony), and moral discourse. Functions as both a sincere assertion and a rhetorical marker. | [CORE] |
| για την αλήθεια | ya tin alíthia | για (for) + την αλήθεια (the truth) | for the sake of truth, to be honest, truthfully | A fixed prepositional phrase used as a discourse marker to signal that the speaker is about to say something frank or corrective. Common in everyday speech and informal writing. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια να λέμε | alíthia na léme | αλήθεια (truth) + να (subjunctive particle) + λέμε (we say) | to tell the truth, honestly speaking, let's be honest | A fixed colloquial expression used to introduce a frank or candid statement. Functions as a hedging or framing device in everyday conversation and informal writing. | [CORE] |
| κατά την αλήθεια | katá tin alíthia | κατά (according to) + την αλήθεια (the truth) | in truth, truthfully, to tell the truth | A formal or literary adverbial phrase used to introduce a candid or corrective statement. More elevated in register than η αλήθεια είναι ότι. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια ή ψέμα | alíthia í pséma | αλήθεια (truth) + ή (or) + ψέμα (lie) | truth or lie; true or false | Used as a binary framing in everyday speech and in game contexts. Also used rhetorically to demand a definitive answer. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια ή τόλμη | alíthia í tólmi | αλήθεια (truth) + ή (or) + τόλμη (dare, boldness) | truth or dare | The name of the party game "truth or dare" as used in Greek. A direct calque of the English game name, but using the native αλήθεια. Used in everyday speech especially among younger speakers. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια και ψέμα | alíthia ke pséma | αλήθεια (truth) + και (and) + ψέμα (lie) | truth and lies; truth and falsehood | A paired formula used to frame a binary opposition between truthfulness and deception. Common in everyday speech, journalism, and moral discourse. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια και δικαιοσύνη | alíthia ke dhikiosíni | αλήθεια (truth) + και (and) + δικαιοσύνη (justice) | truth and justice | A paired formula used in legal, political, and moral discourse to invoke the twin values of truthfulness and fairness. Appears in official documents, political rhetoric, ethical discourse, and the names of political organizations. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια και συμφιλίωση | alíthia ke simfiliosi | αλήθεια (truth) + και (and) + συμφιλίωση (reconciliation) | truth and reconciliation | Used in political and transitional justice contexts, often in reference to truth and reconciliation commissions. A calque of the international term. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια του Θεού | alíthia tu Theú | αλήθεια (truth) + του Θεού (of God, gen.) | God's truth, the truth of God, the absolute truth | Used in religious discourse and as an emphatic oath in everyday speech. "Αλήθεια του Θεού!" is used to swear that something is absolutely true. | [CORE] |
| αλήθεια ενώπιον Θεού | alíthia enópion Theú | αλήθεια (truth) + ενώπιον (before, in the presence of) + Θεού (God, genitive) | truth before God | A religious and legal formula used in oath-taking and solemn declarations to invoke divine witness to the truthfulness of a statement. Appears in ecclesiastical and formal legal contexts. | [MARGINAL] |
| αληθινός Θεός | alithinós Theós | αληθινός (true, genuine) + Θεός (God) | the true God | Used in Christian theological and liturgical discourse to distinguish the God of Christian faith from false gods or idols. Appears in the Nicene Creed and other liturgical texts. | [CORE] |
| αληθής αξία | alithís aksía | αληθής (true) + αξία (value) | true value, real value | Used in financial, economic, and philosophical contexts to refer to the actual or intrinsic value of something as opposed to its nominal or market value. | [CORE] |
| αληθής αγάπη | alithís agápi | αληθής (true) + αγάπη (love) | true love | Used in literary, religious, and everyday contexts to describe love that is genuine and deep as opposed to superficial or feigned. Common in both secular and Christian discourse. | [CORE] |
